125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife.
  • It has been revealed that the discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region.
  • A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife. Researchers have uncovered ancient stone tools, fossils of large animals, and rare plant remains that offer an unusually detailed look at how early humans survived in this dramatically different environment.

It has been revealed that the discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region. Revealed by the Saudi Heritage Commission, the findings are the result of a joint investigation involving the Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University. Published in Science, the research brings together specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, along with experts from several international institutions. Their work provides important fresh evidence about prehistoric human activity, environmental change, and early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.

Sources indicate that today, much of this region is dominated by desert, but the landscape looked very different during the last Interglacial period, around 125,000 years ago. This warm, humid chapter of Arabian history is often called Green Arabia, a time when plentiful water and vegetation supported large animals and human populations.

Recent findings suggest that using satellite-based terrain modeling, scientists reconstructed an enormous ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers. The lake reached depths of up to 29 meters. Evidence from sediments, the surrounding landscape, and the remains of aquatic organisms indicates that it was a relatively stable freshwater environment bordered by open grasslands and vegetation.

In a recent development, the researchers identified more than 500 plant and animal fossil specimens, including invertebrates, spread across more than 130 locations. Among the animals that once inhabited the area were hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. These discoveries reveal a rich prehistoric ecosystem that bears little resemblance to the dry landscape found there today.

Thousands of Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Human Ingenuity.

Alongside the fossils, archaeologists recovered 5,511 stone tools measuring more than 2 centimeters from the main excavation area. More than 98% were made from flint, and analysis demonstrated that the people who created them used Levallois techniques, a method of shaping stone to produce carefully prepared flakes.

To better understand how the tools were made and used, researchers conducted systematic surveys using a grid system to document and collect artifacts and fossils. They also applied two dating methods to sand and fossil teeth, used three-dimensional techniques to determine how stone fragments fit together, and examined tool surfaces with microscopic and chemical analyses.

According to recent reports, these investigations uncovered intriguing evidence of how early humans used the plants around them. Residues preserved on stone tools included traces from several types of vegetation, some of which contain toxic compounds. Resin and woody material suggest that certain stone tips were attached to handles or shafts to make hunting weapons.

Industry observers note that other plant residues point to the processing of tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. This suggests that the people living around the lake relied on vegetation for a variety of purposes, from obtaining food to carrying out everyday activities.

In a recent development, perhaps most surprisingly, the findings raise the possibility that prehistoric hunters incorporated poisonous plant compounds into their hunting technology. Although this interpretation remains tentative, it represents some of the earliest potential evidence of such practices identified in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region's earliest known evidence of palm-related vegetation.

A Rare Glimpse Into Everyday Life 125,000 Years Ago.

What makes Uruq al-Julaybah especially valuable is the unusual combination of discoveries preserved at one location. The animal fossils, manufactured tools, and plant remains were all recovered from the same dated archaeological setting (animal remains, stone tools, and plant material), allowing scientists to piece together a remarkably complete picture of prehistoric life.

The shores of ancient Lake Mundafan appear to have provided an ideal gathering place for early humans. Freshwater, animals, vegetation, and materials suitable for making tools were all available in the surrounding landscape.

Sources indicate that evidence suggests that people used this environment for numerous activities, including manufacturing stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animals and plants, and working with plant fibers. Taken together, the discoveries indicate that these early populations were highly adaptable and made sophisticated use of the resources available to them.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a Heritage Commission researcher and professor of Paleolithic archaeology who participated in the project, emphasized the importance of the discovery at Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter. He described it as a significant archaeological find that helps explain how the ancient environment shaped the lives of humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia during early prehistory.

Reconstructing a Forgotten Chapter of Human History.

"This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," stated Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University's Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. "The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.".

According to recent reports, by bringing together different kinds of archaeological and environmental evidence, the researchers have reconstructed a period of Arabian history that is difficult to imagine from the region's present-day appearance. Their findings offer notable clues about how early humans moved across the Arabian Peninsula, developed technology, and adapted their behavior to changing environmental conditions.

In a recent development, "Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories," remarked Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

In a recent development, the investigation reflects an extensive international research effort to better understand the Arabian Peninsula's ancient human and environmental history. The Saudi Heritage Commission supported fieldwork during the 2023 season, helped fund the research, and facilitated scientific activities.

Along with KAUST, Griffith University in Australia, and King Saud University, the project involved international universities and research centers specializing in archaeology, ancient environments, history, and laboratory analysis. This collaboration demonstrates how combining expertise from different scientific fields can uncover extraordinary details about human life thousands of generations in the past.

#105206. A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1977 w)

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains.
  • Sources indicate that in the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV.
  • It has been revealed that although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL.

Sources indicate that in the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

It has been revealed that although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

Sources indicate that “We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” states Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”.

Recent findings suggest that this year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” states Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

In a recent development, success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” indicates Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

According to recent reports, the latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

According to recent reports, one overarching problem, notes Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” indicates Burton.

Recent findings suggest that researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, indicates Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Sources indicate that source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Industry observers note that sanders notes that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Sources indicate that researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, notes virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979.

According to recent reports, pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.

Recent findings suggest that reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers.

Industry observers note that avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month.

Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the Upcoming Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers.

A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a massive X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing.

The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines).

As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion.

Recent findings suggest that doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant, you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. We won't complain.

Avengers: Doomsday won't fix all of the Multiverse Saga's shortcomings, but at the very least, it looks like a proper fun time with more toys being mashed together than ever before and proper stakes.

Right before Christmas, it's hard to resist such a pitch.

Avengers: Doomsday assembles on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas...Yes, it opens the same day as Dune: Part Three.

Apple's next iPhone release (probably) isn't until sometime next year, but that doesn't mean leaks aren't coming in hot and ready for our perusal.

The latest leak about Apple's flagship hardware product concerns the rumored iPhone 18e. According to digital renders of the device seen by Engadget, you can expect the next budget iPhone to have a camera bump that looks quite different from the iPhone 17e that launched earlier this year.

While the 17e has only a single camera lens flush with the phone's back, Engadget's source suggests that Apple is looking to give the 18e a camera plateau similar to the one on the iPhone Pro models.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean it will allegedly house the camera lens in a nearly square-shaped module measuring about 28 by 35mm. Alongside the lens, the housing will contain the LED flash and a rear microphone. Yes, to be as abundantly clear as possible, Apple is apparently still sticking with just one camera lens here, even if the phone might look like it has more going on back there this time around.

According to recent reports, interestingly, Engadget's report goes further, as they also saw renders of the still-not-available base iPhone 18 and the next iPhone Air. The iPhone 18 reportedly looks similar to previous models, with a thicker camera module. However, the iPhone Air 2 renders show a second camera lens on that phone. As you may or may not recall, the previous iPhone Air model only had one lens, so that would be a pretty substantial upgrade for that device.

It has been revealed that we don't know for certain when these devices will actually launch, but previous reporting suggests that we should see some or all of them by the end of March 2027. They may or may not launch alongside a fresh MacBook Neo and some new iPad models.

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical matter" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank mentioned a "temporary problem related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson stated in a statement to CNBC.

Industry observers note that "This is not a systemic matter — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson noted. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.".

CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.

Recent findings suggest that still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET.

A representative for U.S. Bank said that manufacturer was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.".

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that NASA has released a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.

It has been revealed that "We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," mentioned NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.".

NASA's Plans for a Permanent Moon Base.

NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an notable step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.

"As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.".

Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon.

Sources indicate that the competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.

Recent findings suggest that each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore new approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.

Industry observers note that the challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.

Students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.

Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers.

Sources indicate that beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.

It has been revealed that "Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," mentioned Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge.

According to recent reports, interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.

NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance.

A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history.

As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday, was a “major joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute.

#105193. Breaking: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1210 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
  • After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU remarked it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.
  • "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU remarked it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," mentioned Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required.".

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

Industry observers note that "Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation noted.

According to recent reports, the Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠remarked the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing. Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted latest adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs.".

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, mentioned TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed intends for a global transformation.".

In a recent development, at the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such looks as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

According to recent reports, it included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

Industry observers note that the talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot.".

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”.

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that another contenious glitch at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text stated the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve.".

Industry observers note that the stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, mentioned his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation.".

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks.
  • According to recent reports, this initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings.
  • "Our aim right now is to gather the substantial-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.

According to recent reports, this initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.

"Our aim right now is to gather the substantial-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.".

"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!".

Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids.

Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.

It has been revealed that with gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling quickly across the ground.

Rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an key safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.

Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids.

Sources indicate that next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.

The mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.

Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Sources indicate that the mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.

Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision.

Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.

The impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.

However, the experiment also raised important questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?

Industry observers note that researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.

These details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.

A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.

According to recent reports, the spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.

In a recent development, together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.

Bellingham has scored seven goals this season but this will be one to remember.

Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV.

Mourinho opted to leave the England midfielder out of the starting line-up for Tuesday's Champions League game at the Bernabeu - an understandable decision given the demands of Madrid's fixture schedule and the strength in depth at his disposal.

But after watching his side trail 1-0 at half-time against the Dutch side, Mourinho knew changes were needed.

"He is an amazing player that has everything," the Portuguese manager mentioned. "He has physicality, he understands the game, he has absolutely everything. Today, he has changed how the game was evolving.".

Captain Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute and 10 minutes later Bellingham produced his moment of magic.

Receiving the ball just outside the penalty area, he took two touches to lift it into position before unleashing a magnificent volley with the outside of his right foot, leaving PSV keeper Matej Kovar with no chance.

It was a sensational finish, executed with extraordinary precision.

It has been revealed that "I was a bit surprised, honestly," Bellingham said about the goal. "I knew that I could control the ball well and get it into my grasp. But normally from there, I'm looking to see who's on as an option to play through.

According to recent reports, "It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and key for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control.".

The 23-year-old celebrated in trademark fashion, standing with his arms outstretched in front of the home supporters as thousands serenaded him with chants of 'Hey Jude'.

It was his fourth goal in his past five appearances for Real.

Asked whether he should be compared to Real and France legend Zinedine Zidane, who won the Ballon d'Or and World Cup in 1998, Bellingham maintained his humility.

In a recent development, "I think Zidane is much better than me. He's much more elegant and he's my idol," he said.

'I'm just going to hit it!' - Bellingham reacts to stunning goal.

Kylian Mbappe scored two more goals and Vinicius Junior put away the fifth to complete a super turnaround from a team that had looked short of ideas in the first half.

At the suggestion that he is at the moment in the form of his life, Bellingham said: "I think you're only as good as your next one [game]. Your last one doesn't really matter.

"But my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game. Thinking about my best form or being the best player in the world doesn't mean anything to me.".

For Bellingham, the ability to respond when things are not going according to initiative is what separates the best teams from the rest.

"We're managing to show that mentality that good teams do, that even if you're not playing well, you can raise the level at any point," he remarked.

His adaptation to life in Spain has also been an important part of that journey.

Asked about his increasingly impressive Spanish, Bellingham admitted he still gets nervous when speaking the language in public.

According to recent reports, "It's getting a little bit better. I get a little bit nervous speaking to you guys. It's much easier in the changing room," he joked to journalists.

According to recent reports, "I'm loving living in Spain. I'm loving the club. I think for English players it's such an notable thing to go and move abroad and learn newly introduced things and I've obviously benefited massively from that.".

And while his performances have inevitably brought renewed attention to individual awards, Bellingham remarked that personal recognition is not what motivates him.

Asked about the Ballon d'Or, he mentioned his focus was only on the team.

"I don't care about the Ballon d'Or, honestly. I want to win a lot of titles with the team, the Champions League, the League.".

"The Ballon d'Or is something for you, journalists, to vote and create a bit of tension. But for me it's more key that the team win.".

Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.
  • While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.
  • In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

Industry observers note that NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Recent findings suggest that curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

In a recent development, data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Recent findings suggest that together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

Latest Update: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems.
  • Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling.
  • In a recent development, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

The research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," states senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use.".

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation.".

Why Moon Bases Need Tougher Insulation.

Designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

Some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

Another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

According to recent reports, strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

Sources indicate that "For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.".

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation.

Recent findings suggest that the Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

Sources indicate that rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

Industry observers note that assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," says Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.".

Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

Additional mechanical testing showed that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability.

According to recent reports, one of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

In a recent development, the samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

It has been revealed that "We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row.".

It has been revealed that this resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, debuted, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

Recent findings suggest that durability would remain important after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really notable to have tough materials that can last long enough.".

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer.

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an key clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

According to recent reports, the discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

In a recent development, that result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better.

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

In a recent development, at first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

According to recent reports, the finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," says Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.".

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases.

Although the early results are encouraging, the newly introduced insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

It has been revealed that the experimental HyLIFS samples presently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

To make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

Notable questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

Sources indicate that for Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she notes.

Recent findings suggest that the research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.

Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

#105181. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty.
  • In a recent development, A upcoming study suggests they become more likely to follow.
  • They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

In a recent development, A upcoming study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group.".

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

It has been revealed that small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

In a recent development, people also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

Industry observers note that in some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

Molleman calls the work fundamental science and states the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he stated that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

It has been revealed that after launching the Upcoming Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Blue Origin's Fresh Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

It has been revealed that since that first landing, Blue Origin has introduced 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The manufacturer reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical concern.) But in January 2026, the company unveiled a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

Sources indicate that but Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the manufacturer's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.
