📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • Industry observers note that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • In a recent development, the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

Industry observers note that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results indicated that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

In a recent development, the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

According to recent reports, the second state was particularly crucial because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," claims senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely newly introduced electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Sources indicate that future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Viktor Gyokeres has scored three goals in all competitions this season for Arsenal.

It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.

In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal.

The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years.

But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game.

Sources indicate that against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.

They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes.

In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target.

Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance".

"The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition that we played today and what we've done out there, is just something to be very, very pleased [about] because there is very little more that you can demand from the team," Arteta noted.

"But obviously, the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance in the amount of chances (and) situations.

It has been revealed that "There is an element of luck; there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist because I think what the team has done and shown today, I think it's the right direction.".

Arsenal held by Borussia Dortmund in Champions League.

Arteta made six changes to the side that drew with Newcastle, with one of the biggest calls to rest striker Kai Havertz and bring in Viktor Gyokeres.

The striker has had a difficult season so far, with four of his seven starts coming in the Champions League against opposition where Arsenal have been favourites.

However, Gyokeres scored a powerful effort from outside the area to give Arsenal the lead against Dortmund.

Overall though, it ended up being a mixed night for the 28-year-old as he missed a header from inside the six-yard-box that would have surely won the game for the Gunners late on.

Arteta was asked if the chances his side are missing were down to mentality, misfortune or composure.

"Mentality, I don't know," he stated.

"There is an element of luck here because how some of the goals they haven't gone inside, I don't know.

"The execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think it was really, really good.".

Arteta was also full of praise for Gyokeres, with particular emphasis on the striker's link-up play; an element of his game at times criticised.

"What I love the most is how connected he was to the team," Arteta stated.

Recent findings suggest that "We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch.

"There was a lot to like in that performance and that's the Viktor that we needed.".

Noni Madueke has been Arsenal's best attacker in recent weeks.

The winger, who was left out of the last England squad, is enjoying a run in the Arsenal starting XI with Bukayo Saka out injured and is taking his opportunity.

Madueke has registered a goal and two assists in his past three games and was again the best Arsenal forward against Dortmund.

The Gunners host Manchester City on Sunday and are at the moment six points clear at the top of the Premier League table.

Madueke, who was frustrated with the performance against Dortmund, said the clash with third-placed City is a great chance to get back to winning ways and shake off any frustration.

"I think these are the best games. I'm really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same," Madueke told Amazon Prime.

Sources indicate that "We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We're champions, we're at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates.

"There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction.".

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the concerns that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford stated the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the concerns that caused Friday's ground stop.

'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw for Manchester City against Napoli.
  • Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.
  • The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw for Manchester City against Napoli.

Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.

The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.

It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.

Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.

City's recent defensive problems also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.

According to recent reports, maresca mentioned: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end.

"Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on.

It has been revealed that "The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end.".

Individual errors are really costing Man City...

Cherki rescues point for Man City against Napoli.

City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few complications in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.

Their injury problems mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.

They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.

Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.

The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is promptly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes.

"It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend.

"You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out.".

Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.

The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.

The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.

It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net.

"I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy.

It has been revealed that "Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy.".

City are sixth in the Champions League table, before Wednesday's games, but in the Premier League they have failed to win their past four.

It does not get any easier this weekend, facing a daunting trip to leaders Arsenal on Sunday as they aim to find some form.

Haaland added: "It's the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away.

"We need a top performance from every single player.".

#105170. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1272 w)

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • Sources indicate that the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less crucial than how they use that time.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less crucial than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

Sources indicate that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

It has been revealed that cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn newly introduced things, and solve problems. These abilities play an crucial role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

According to recent reports, the findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

In a recent development, "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing upcoming information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

It has been revealed that one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

Industry observers note that "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

Recent findings suggest that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

In a recent development, importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, the results offer an notable perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#105169. Industry News: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1486 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics.
  • Industry observers note that not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.
  • As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics. The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation, the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut.

Industry observers note that not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field.

As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.

We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well.

"First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author.

"'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen.".

In a recent development, in a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height.

Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude.

Industry observers note that of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with maneuvering yourself. Any ball or other object would also be subject to this altered set of physics.

As Johnson points out, "Aside from maneuvering the body and not tumbling or going in the wrong direction, the most difficult part would probably be throwing or hitting a ball in zero g. There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw. That would take getting used to doing, given that we’ve spent our entire lives calculating how high and fast to throw a ball in 1G so it gets to the person we intend.".

Science fiction interpretations have often leaned into these differences; in many cases, low-g sports look more like three-dimensional chess than the highly physical contests we're used to here on Earth.

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

2013's "Ender's Game" gives us one of the best examples of a zero-g arena in space. Dubbed the "Battle Room," it's a giant hollow cube filled with obstacles. Teams enter through gates at opposite ends and participate in laser tag-style drills while having to grapple with three-dimensional space, while also finding ways to propel and protect themselves.

In a recent development, "The Battle Room sequence does a great job of thinking about straight‑line, constant‑velocity motion," Johnson said. "No 'reaction' to slow you down or change your direction. Characters push off walls or each other, then drift until they hit something or fire their suit's thrusters.".

Johnson mentioned Ender's Game also did an admirable job of showcasing how alternate physics require another layer of planning when moving through space.

Industry observers note that "They went to great lengths to show that there was no preferred 'up' or 'down'. Again, very accurate and realistic thinking. Floating obstacles in the battle space created realistic constraints: if you don't think about where you'll rebound, you can pin yourself behind an obstacle or drift out of the fight.".

Recent findings suggest that recognizing how crucial play can be (and, perhaps, acknowledging ways to combat the lingering specter of space madness), real-world space agencies have begun brainstorming what recreation in low gravity might look like. Some proposed ideas include 3D ball games not wholly dissimilar from the Battle Room, where players enter a cube or spherical arena and push off walls/pass a ball in any direction, scoring by hitting targets.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. The Space Games Federation has also floated the idea of a version of space basketball, where the goal is guiding a magnetic ball through hoops, as well as some version of space dodgeball.

Of course, these proposals are nothing more than thought exercises at the moment. We're a long way out from vast human populations living in zero-g environments for extended periods of time, and even further still from building spaceships capable of housing a sports hall.

Industry observers note that NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

Industry observers note that these fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need new rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Sources indicate that games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

In a recent development, the game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs.".

Sources indicate that with that said, there are areas where sci-fi portrayals of zero-G games fall down. Energy levels and fatigue is a major one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the problem of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Industry observers note that johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how rapidly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." He points to incidents where real-life astronauts have demonstrated how challenging this phenomenon would actually be. "I’ve watched many videos of astronauts on the ISS twist and then bounce off the wall or something. They have all looked very clumsy when they do this.".

The other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that said, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this blog is now closed. Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germany on Monday, November 23.

Thank you for following our coverage of headlines from Germany on Monday, November 24.

The Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

In a recent development, from early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

It has been revealed that the Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

Up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

The Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

Industry observers note that the continent’s share of German foreign trade at the moment stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider mentioned: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile.".

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

Industry observers note that speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider noted: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions.".

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures.".

German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which said that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.

The reports stated Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz mentioned not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

US President George W. Bush noted he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France stated that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz said, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented.".

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said.

Merz remarked Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia introduced its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location.".

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also indicated about 300 latest deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They remarked that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police noted they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a newly introduced chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

Sources indicate that A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

Recent findings suggest that the strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it notes was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

According to recent reports, german exports to Africa have reached a latest record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

It has been revealed that the biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

In a recent development, "The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Recent findings suggest that major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention prepares to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

Sources indicate that "I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.
  • Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.
  • Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it demonstrates how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Industry observers note that scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson stated.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage revealed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and stated younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson mentioned, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he noted.

Latest Update: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism revealed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

In a recent development, to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Recent findings suggest that using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

Recent findings suggest that people with autism demonstrated substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

It has been revealed that the results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers now blueprint to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United defender Leny Yoro (second left) is shown a red card by referee Sam Barrott at Anfield.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has questioned the competence of video assistant referee officials after defender Leny Yoro had his red card overturned by the Football Association.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday after bringing down Aleksander Isak just outside the United penalty area.

United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.

Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.

"I am very disappointed," the Argentine stated. "This type of thing can never happen.

Sources indicate that "We can accept the referee can make a mistake. But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? Are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play 11 by 11? No.

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?".

United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.

They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.

It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.

'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned.

Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on 13 September was allowed to stand even though a clearly offside Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play.

There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.

Instead, he has doubled down on the call, saying: "I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.".

United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.

The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.

This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.

Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.

"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," stated Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.

"We need to defend my players and my club, and that is to denounce it and to say, the decision wasn't good. And now, the three points, where are the three points?".

What referee's chief Webb said about the incident on the Mic'd Up programme.

Recent findings suggest that "There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

"That was the referee's call made on the field, and then the VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn't.

"That if there was any doubt, then it was doubt.

It has been revealed that "It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. and.

"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving rapidly on towards that ball.

Sources indicate that "The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable. Certainly not clearly wrong.".

Why was Yoro's red card overturned?

United's fury over Yoro and the way the situation has been handled cannot completely obscure the fact they lost 4-0 in Pochettino's first game in charge.

It extended a terrible start to the season that has seen the Red Devils win on just three occasions - and only once in the Premier League, against newly-promoted Ipswich in August.

The club are 19th in the Premier League and facing up to the possibility of being relegated for the first time since 1973-74.

Yet Pochettino is adamant there is no fragility about his upcoming squad.

Sources indicate that "The situation is fragile in [terms of] the environment, or the people want it to look like we're fragile. But I don't say that we are fragile. I think we are strong.

"We have great mentality and a great mindset.

Sources indicate that "There are many things we need to improve. It's normal to be in a different position, and everyone can use different words to describe the situation.

"But we are a strong team. They demonstrated that last season, capable of finishing third. I think we are going to turn around the situation and start to perform in the level like before Bruno [Fernandes] said, deserve to be at this club.".

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (left) and skipper Bruno Fernandes speak to the media ahead of the Champions League clash with Sporting in Lisbon.

Skipper Bruno Fernandes revealed at the weekend talks over a new United contract were on hold.

The 32-year-old's present deal expires in the summer, although the club have an option to extend it by 12 months.

Speaking alongside Pochettino at a media conference before his first meeting with Sporting since he left to join United in a Â£47m deal in January 2020, Fernandes said his sole focus at present is to drag United out of the mire.

"For us to start winning games, then we can start speaking about contract," he stated.

"It's not important now. It's irrelevant. Obviously, I know it's my future and I probably shouldn't look into that way because I haven't got much left in my contract, but I'm not really worried about that.

"I'm more worried about getting results, trying to bring the club back in a position that we can be proud of, and we're not there at the moment.".

#105158. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1195 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A newly introduced study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

Industry observers note that "The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," remarked Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy reveals up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

According to recent reports, the researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

Sources indicate that after writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

Sources indicate that the analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

In a recent development, boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

In a recent development, these differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

Industry observers note that "What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane noted. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

According to recent reports, the researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

According to recent reports, this variation is key because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

Recent findings suggest that "People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray mentioned. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

In a recent development, "Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

Recent findings suggest that like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Recent findings suggest that recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane noted. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's key to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she noted. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".
